courses.title: Hazmat Awareness — Recertification
courses.summary: Recognize, isolate, and notify. Refresh your decision frame for hazardous-materials incidents.
courses.credibility: Built with NFPA 472 alignment and reviewed by 3 fire-service SMEs.

blocks.body: On arrival, your first 60 seconds are about *recognition*, not action. The placard, container shape, and bystander reports together build the picture.

blocks.prompt: You see a diamond placard with the number 1203 on a tanker. What does that suggest?

options.label: Gasoline (flammable liquid)
options.feedback: Correct — UN 1203 is gasoline. Your isolation distance defaults to 50m and grows with fire involvement.

options.label: Corrosive liquid
options.feedback: Not quite — corrosives use class 8 placards, not UN 1203.

options.label: Compressed oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen is UN 1072 with a class 2.2 (oxidizer) placard.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: On arrival, isolation is a *living* distance — it expands the moment you see vapor, heat, or victim symptoms, and only contracts once monitoring confirms the air. Wind, slope, and bystander position all push the perimeter outward. Treat 50 meters as the *minimum*, not the answer.

items.title: Field note
items.body: Two-thirds of preventable exposures happen in the first 90 seconds because the perimeter wasn't moved when the wind shifted.

blocks.title: Escalation pathway
blocks.body: If the product remains unidentified after 5 minutes, default to Tier 2 isolation (>150m) and request hazmat-1. Don't downgrade until a second confirming observation matches your initial read.
A precise sitrep beats a long one. Lead with location, product, isolation, and resources requested.

courses.title: Critical Thinking — Foundations
courses.summary: Recognize claims, separate evidence from assertion, and structure a defensible argument.
courses.credibility: Reviewed by your faculty advisor; aligned to the campus rhetoric standard.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Every argument has a *claim* (what you assert), *evidence* (what supports it), and a *warrant* (why the evidence proves the claim). Most weak arguments skip the warrant — they show data and hope the connection is obvious.

courses.title: Lockout / Tagout — Refresher
courses.summary: Six-step LOTO sequence, energy-isolation verification, and exception handling for shift transitions.
courses.credibility: OSHA 1910.147-aligned; reviewed by site EHS lead.

blocks.title: Notify, shut down, isolate, lock, dissipate, verify
Procedural overview
blocks.body: LOTO is six steps in order — *notify, shut down, isolate, lock, dissipate, verify*. Skipping verify is the failure mode behind most stored-energy injuries: the device is locked, but the system still has potential energy waiting to release.

blocks.body: qSOFA isn't a diagnosis — it's a flag. Two of three (RR≥22, altered mentation, SBP≤100) raises the bar for re-eval, not for protocol auto-launch.

courses.title: Patient Assessment on a Routine Call
courses.summary: Run a single-patient medical call cleanly — scene safety, vitals, communication.
courses.credibility: Aligned to NREMT assessment objectives; reviewed by your training officer.

blocks.title: First 30 seconds on a medical call
What you're looking for
blocks.body: Before you touch the patient, you're reading the scene: hazards, mechanism, number of patients, and your team's lane. The work is observation, not action — your job in the first half-minute is to *not get hurt* and to set the tone for the patient.

blocks.title: ABC, vitals, and the focused history
Procedural overview
blocks.body: Run airway, breathing, circulation in that order, then a quick set of vitals. Don't skip rate, quality, and rhythm — those three together do more diagnostic work than any single number.

blocks.prompt: A conscious adult patient with chest pain is breathing 18, pulse 88 strong and regular, BP 132/84. Your next move?

options.label: Start a focused history (OPQRST) while continuing to monitor
options.feedback: Right — they're stable. The chest pain history is what shapes treatment from here.

options.label: Apply oxygen immediately at 15L/min
options.feedback: No clinical indication. Routine high-flow O2 in a stable patient can do harm.

options.label: Move directly to transport without further assessment
options.feedback: You'd be transporting without the information that shapes destination and report.

blocks.title: When the picture is changing faster than you can read it
The frame
blocks.body: Under load, your job is to *narrow* the field, not widen it. Pick the next-best action you can defend in 10 seconds, commit, and re-read. Indecision burns more time than an imperfect choice.

courses.title: Evaluating Sources for a Research Assignment
courses.summary: Tell credible sources from questionable ones — fast, repeatedly, before they enter your draft.
courses.credibility: Aligned to your library's research guide.

blocks.title: What to scan before you read
Procedural overview
blocks.body: Before you read a source, do a fast credibility scan: who wrote it, what are they citing, when was it published, and what's the venue. If any of those four are murky, your bar to use it goes up.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Every source has a viewpoint. The question isn't *whether* a source is biased — it's whether the bias is disclosed, whether the evidence still holds, and whether you can triangulate with a counter-view.

courses.title: Hazard Recognition on the Floor
courses.summary: Spot the hazards that get walked past every day — and decide when to flag, fix, or escalate.
courses.credibility: OSHA-aligned; reviewed by site EHS lead.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Most preventable incidents come from hazards that someone *almost* reported. Train your eyes on the boring stuff: a loose cord, a missing label, a fan running on a wet floor. The boring stuff is the data.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Three options every time: *flag* (log it, tell the shift lead), *fix* (only if it's in your scope and you can verify), or *escalate* (any energy source, any chemical, any injury). When in doubt, escalate.

blocks.title: Tone, timing, and the screenshot rule
What to do first
blocks.body: When someone sends a message that feels off — mean, weird, or just wrong — your first move is *pause and screenshot*. Don't reply yet. The message can't take itself back; you can decide how to respond after you've shown an adult.

lessons.title: Making the call on a tool

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Before you use an AI tool or share a doc, ask three questions: *Is it allowed for this class? Does it credit the original work? Would the teacher recognize your contribution?* If any answer is no, change course.

courses.title: Recognizing & Reporting Concerns
courses.summary: Spot early warning signs in students and route them through your reporting path.
courses.credibility: Aligned to your state's mandated-reporter statute and district policy.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Recognition isn't about being right — it's about being early. Any single sign can have a benign explanation; the work is to notice a *cluster* (mood + attendance + a comment + a parent change) and lower your threshold to ask, not to wait until you're sure.

blocks.title: Procedural overview
blocks.body: Mandated reporting doesn't require certainty — it requires *reasonable suspicion*. If you're talking yourself out of reporting, that's the cue to report. The system, not you, decides what comes next.
